items.title: 🔓 [Fast Company] Raising kids has gotten so expensive, parents are turning to an unexpected lifeline
items.content_html:
🎨 🌾 🔧 🪶 🌲 🏔️ 🔭 ✏️

More than 3 in 4 parents say relying on Boomer grandparents is essential to afford raising kids

Raising children is becoming more and more costly, and modern parents are feeling the strain. Now, according to one new report, grown adults with children are relying on their own parents in high numbers.

The data comes from a survey of 2,500 U.S. adults by the global market research company Ipsos for the 2026 BMO Real Financial Progress Index. The research found that the large majority of parents in the U.S. believe that the cost of raising children is “out of control,” with 82% agreeing with the sentiment. Meanwhile, even nonparents are concerned about the cost of raising children, as 79% wonder how their peers can afford to have families. 

“Raising kids has always been a labor of love, but right now, it is also a major feat of financial engineering with families torn between spending on the urgent and the important,” Robin Growley, U.S. Head of Consumer Products, BMO, said in a news release.

Growley continued, “Whether you are budgeting for diapers or dorm rooms, the absolute best antidote to daily financial stress is a clear, actionable plan.” 

For many modern parents, part of the plan seems to be relying on their own boomer parents to afford raising their kids. In 2026, 76% of parents with children under 18 say that receiving financial support from extended family is necessary to afford opportunities for their children. Likewise, 37% of parents expect financial help from their parents or grandparents over the next year and plan to ask for it. 

Mostly, that group is getting help with daily living expenses. 47% of those who will ask for help say they will receive cash for their everyday needs. 43% say the help will come in the form of free childcare, provided by grandparents, or help with the costs of childcare. 26% say their family is helping financially by putting away funds for the future for their children.

The need for financial assistance isn’t due to the fact that modern parents are lazy or wildly over-spending. Mainly, it has to do with how quickly the cost of raising children has gone up drastically in recent years. According to a 2026 Lending Tree analysis, since 2023, the annual cost of raising a young child has skyrocketed by nearly 36%, coming to about $30,000 per year, or $300,000 over 18 years. 

Interestingly, while financial help from family may go a long way, there’s an emotional tax that comes with it. Those who live close to aging parents and receive help with the costs of raising children are more likely financially overwhelmed than those who don’t (74% as opposed to 57%).  

Growley noted that the numbers likely reflect the sandwich generation’s attunement with the fact that their parents raising children also realize their aging parents will soon be relying on them, too. “Having a grandparent help raise your kids can be one of life’s greatest gifts, but family caregiving is often a reciprocal arrangement—and it can be a lot when you’re already stretched thin,” Growley said.

items.title: [Kottke.org] A Deep Dive Into the Full Bayeux Tapestry Story
items.content_html:
From Deep Down History, an entertaining hour-long explainer video on the Bayeux Tapestry.

This video tells the Tapestry’s story in full, using Charles Stothard’s early colour reproduction, presented here as a seamless scroll for the first time. We follow Harold Godwinson’s fateful journey from Edward the Confessor’s court to Normandy, his later seizure of the Crown, and William the Conqueror’s invasion. Beyond its political messaging, the Tapestry is also bursting with medieval history, including jokes, fascinating technical details, and a warning for those who break their promises…

Completed within a decade or two of the events which it depicts, the tapestry is back in the news & public consciousness because it’s back in England for the first time since it was made and on display at the British Museum.

items.title: 🔓 [Fast Company] A cure for physician burnout is better use of patient data
items.content_html:
🎨 🔧 🌲 🏔️ 🔭 ✏️

🎨 🔧 🌲 🏔️ 🔭 ✏️

🎨 🔧 🌲 🏔️ 🔭 ✏️

Somewhere in America, a physician is trying to reconstruct where their patient has been for the last six months. A hospital admission in March, a discharge to a rehabilitation facility, and then the specialist follow-up that may or may not have happened, with a medication list that is out of date. The patient does their best to fill in the gaps from memory. The office visit is only 12 minutes long, and most of it is spent on detective work.

When the visit is over, the doctor returns to endless bureaucratic tasks, having spent more time digging through records and charting than caring for the patient. Members of today’s patient care continuum, like primary care, pharmacy, specialists, home health, skilled nursing, and beyond, operate on siloed, disconnected information systems that create an immense amount of inefficient work. As a result, primary care physicians spend more than half of their workday on computer-based electronic health record (EHR) tasks.

This never-ending “type‑and‑click” work is a major driver of physician burnout, which can lead to medical errors, decreased care quality, safety incidents, and reduced patient satisfaction. Some physician burnout rates are nearly 50%. The strain does not come from EHRs alone; time pressure, chaotic workplaces, low control of work pace, and organizational culture further exacerbate conditions.

In response, physicians are leaving the industry at an alarming rate. In another AMA survey, more than 35% noted interest in leaving their jobs in the next two years. The U.S. can’t stand to lose that many physicians, as the country is already projected to face a shortage of up to 86,000 physicians by 2036.

RUDDERLESS PATIENT DATA CREATES BURDEN

Health systems generate more patient data than most physicians can ever see. Unfortunately, it sits idle across disparate systems. Primary care physicians aren’t notified when one of their patients goes to the ER and requires a follow-up. A skilled nursing facility isn’t made aware of a prescription change that puts an elderly patient at risk of a dangerous medication interaction.

In our work with providers, we have found that poorly designed digital tools leave them with less time for patients and more time chasing the information they need to avoid these issues. Physicians frequently share that interoperability gaps and clunky design can affect their performance and increase patient safety risks.

One analysis found that stress from technologies, chronic time pressure, and persistent workflow issues greatly contribute to clinician burnout. Because multiple EHRs cannot easily share or interpret data, clinicians must hunt through information trails with faxes and phone calls to compile complete health pictures before making care decisions. The case for connected and actionable patient data is paramount to supporting providers’ mental health, helping them close frequent issue points, and addressing some of the main contributors to physician burnout.

SHELVE THE MINDFULNESS APPS AND PUT PATIENT DATA TO BETTER USE

People tend to categorize physician burnout as a resilience problem, something that mindfulness apps, wellness stipends, and protected lunch hours can fix. But those are band-aids. The real answer is cutting physicians’ endless hours at the keyboard by adopting technology that shares patient data among every provider who touches a patient’s care, including public health and community partners, so physicians easily understand the full health picture and receive real-time alerts on what matters most for their patients.

When data moves with the patient, each visit in the care journey changes its shape. A physician gets pinged the moment their patient lands in the hospital, knows exactly where they went after discharge, and can intercede before the next hospital readmission instead of after one. The 12-minute visit becomes 12 minutes of actual medicine instead of fatiguing detective work.

Effie Carlson is the CEO of Watershed Health and Monica Rivera, MD, MPH is the chief growth officer of Watershed Health.

items.title: 🔓 [Fast Company] The last mile for public policy
items.content_html:
Governments ultimately deliver outcomes through thousands of people making decisions at local government, nonprofits, and service provider organizations. Technical assistance is how those decisions improve over time.

In theory, technical assistance is simple: make sure the people implementing policy know what to do, and how, with advice and guidance from state and federal agencies. It’s one of the most important aspects of how government agencies operate.

But government employees I’ve spoken with acknowledge that the status quo of how TA is delivered is fundamentally broken.

IT HAPPENS EVERY DAY

Imagine a federal program with millions of dollars in grants to disburse to state and local agencies. Before a dollar moves, program staff must define which entities are eligible, build a rubric, identify the metrics that define success and community impact, and align stakeholders across thousands of organizations nationwide. Then they must make potential grantees aware of the grant.

A significant share of that upstream work is time spent interviewing people and defining criteria. It’s careful, expensive work. And none of it matters if the dollars don’t reach the organizations that can improve the lives of the people the grant was written for.

FROM POLICY TO ACTION

Every major government initiative depends on hundreds or thousands of implementing partners from local government agencies and nonprofits to service providers.

For example, a state board of elections spends significant time advising election clerks on hiring and recruiting, advocating for rule changes with the state government, and helping educate the public about local election processes. The same is true for public health programs, veterans’ programs, homelessness coordination, and dozens of other initiatives. Technical assistance makes these programs possible, but it is delivered ad hoc, typically at a single point in time, rather than continuously meeting ongoing needs.

3 BROKEN ELEMENTS

Today’s approach to delivering technical assistance results in bottlenecks that prevent expertise from reaching the practitioners who need it when they need it.

  1. It doesn’t scale. As provider networks grow in complexity, the people with the answers become single points of failure. Professional staff burn time managing unwieldy contact lists and answering the same question repeatedly. Support becomes uneven and some organizations never get help.
  1. It falls short when it’s needed most. Service providers need technical assistance during implementation or when working through an edge case, not just at kickoff. Without current guidance, providers fall back on what they already know, which renders the upfront investment in knowledge sharing moot. Meanwhile, guidance gets buried in inboxes and shared drives, and knowledge walks out the door when a state or federal employee leaves.
  1. It’s opaque. Agency leaders struggle to see which providers are receiving assistance, how engaged partners are across the ecosystem, or where implementation is systemically breaking down. Problems surface after a missed deadline, when it is too late.

As federal policy continues to shift and states and local governments contend with budget cuts and turnover, technical assistance capacity doesn’t scale linearly with headcount.

TECHNOLOGY FOR TECHNICAL ASSISTANCE

The bulk of investment in TA programs goes to consulting engagements and professional services. Consultants have expertise and they get the content right. Where TA falls short is delivery and resilience. Without a real-time connection across the network—one that keeps knowledge from fragmenting when a contract ends—technical assistance can’t do what it’s supposed to do.

Hiring more consultants is a temporary fix. And like many state and local programs, TA runs on outdated tools and the elbow grease of already overworked public servants.

Public servants are often technologically lacking in comparison to their private sector peers, through no fault of their own. Trying to create a real-time ecosystem of people involved in TA for a program—and similar programs—requires more than listservs and spreadsheets.

Modern software that’s purpose-built for interagency collaboration, communication, and the knowledge-sharing work central to technical assistance represents a fundamental shift from a series of disconnected, point-in-time activities to lasting implementation infrastructure.

Tools built for TA must meet two requirements. First, they must capture intelligence from across the network. The answer to a question from a nonprofit employee in one county is probably useful to a local government employee on the other side of the state. Rather than remaining siloed, that knowledge bridges jurisdictional gaps and connects everyone involved in delivering a service.

Second, tools built for TA must preserve institutional memory. Instead of an answer languishing in one person’s inbox, it’s available to everyone in the ecosystem—and to everyone working on a similar initiative years from now.

Together, those two capabilities represent technical assistance as a virtuous loop. Rather than experts pushing out ad hoc information, they can see what the field is asking, provide better answers, and get sharper questions in return.

Layering AI onto the structured loop of TA data makes it possible to answer routine questions instantly while surfacing emerging implementation challenges back to program staff. Every interaction strengthens the knowledge available to the entire network.

A STANDING CAPABILITY

We must shift from treating technical assistance as a deliverable to treating it as a capability. A deliverable has a start date, an end date, and a final invoice. A capability persists. It gets stronger the more people use it, and it survives the turnover, budget cycles, and contract expirations that currently erase institutional memory every few years.

That distinction matters more now than it did five years ago. Federal requirements are shifting, budgets are volatile, and the people who know how programs work are retiring. Agencies can’t hire their way through that. But they can build a system where an answer given once is available to everyone who needs it next.

Madeleine Smith is the cofounder and CEO of Civic Roundtable.

items.title: 🔓 [Fast Company] How to support a colleague who has lost a loved one to suicide
items.content_html:
🎨 🔧 ✏️

🎨 🔧 ✏️

🎨 🔧 ✏️

🎨 🔧 ✏️

🎨 🔧 ✏️

In 2024 almost 50,000 Americans died by suicide, making it the 10th leading cause of death in the United States. And the ripple effects are even wider. According to research, each suicide is connected to 135 people who knew the deceased, including coworkers, along with a percentage of those who were considered “close connections.” Extrapolating that data, 6.6 million people are added to the larger community of suicide loss survivors each year.

I am one of those “loss survivors.” On January 5, 2025, while in a plane taxiing out on a runway, I received a text message from my half-brother telling me my father had died by suicide. The shock of his death, including how it was communicated, left me traumatized and depressed. While I was fortunate to have the strong support of my wife, daughter, and son-in-law, at some point I started to think, “Who should I tell?”

While the decision about sharing the loss of my father was highly personal and based on a number of factors, which I discussed with my grief therapist, it left me thinking, How can we support others in the workplace who have faced these unimaginable events in their lives? And that commitment is not one to be taken lightly, given the stigma of suicide, linked to effects that research lists as “concealment of the death, social withdrawal, reduced psychological and somatic functioning, and grief difficulties.”

The strategies here are designed as suggestions to help others who might want support but who might not ask for it. I would like to thank all of the mental health specialists and corporate leaders who agreed to be interviewed for this article.

I am not a mental health professional, and this is not mental health advice, but here are some approaches to your colleague who might not be ready, prepared, or equipped to share the grief and sense of loss that comes with the suicide of a loved one. 

Start with condolences

A good first step is to offer your condolences, delicately and respectfully. One person I interviewed, whose mother died by suicide, said, “A few of my colleagues handed me cards with handwritten notes of condolence. I will never forget how thoughtful that was, that they took the time to write a note of kindness.” I also experienced something similar, and will never forget those who took the time to be so mindful and respectful. Sure, email is always an option, but a deeper sense of sympathy is conveyed by a meaningful card with a handwritten note of condolences and support, beyond a simple signature.

By conveying condolences, without mentioning anything specific and respecting your colleague’s privacy, you allow the person who is grieving, as one mental health specialist stated, “to retain their own narrative without feeling like someone is being presumptive. Such gestures also convey availability and humanity without any assumption of a reply or explanation.” 

Offering further support

To gauge how to respond, you need to consider your relationship with the individual. Are they a colleague with whom you have little social connection other than work-related interactions, or a close coworker and friend you socialize with? How you decide to express your regrets should tie into that relationship.

If you don’t have a close relationship but work in the same office, a simple expression of regret or a note of support would be appreciated, demonstrating that even though you might not be particularly close, you care about your coworker and the death of their loved one. One person I interviewed told how such a work acquaintance sent a flower arrangement to their coworker’s desk, a touching gesture of support. “The fact that we were not particularly close, but he still took the time to send me some flowers, was extremely touching,” he said.

In the case of a close coworker, consider offering more support. As one corporate leader told me when such a coworker’s loved one died by suicide, “I didn’t want to just offer my condolences, I wanted to offer her my company, so I invited her to a tea outside the office, to give her a moment of respite from the stress of returning to work and to just take a break.” That invitation gave her colleague the liberty to share but without any imposition or intrusion. The corporate leader added, “My friend was just appreciative that I took her out of the office environment, and even for a brief moment, to feel that she could just converse and it didn’t have to be about her grief.”

However, keep in mind even a close colleague may not be prepared to talk about what happened. If a grieving colleague doesn’t want to engage, respect their boundaries. Especially shortly after someone’s death and the return to work,  there are strong reasons why your colleague might not want to engage more specifically, beyond accepting your condolences. Those reasons include:

  • Confusion around how the death occurred. “How could this have happened?”
  • Self-scrutiny and self-blame: “Should I have done more?”
  • Anger. “How could they have done that to us?”
  • Religious objections and guilt. 
  • Shame: “I never thought I would have this in my life.”

If your colleague does want more support 

Grief is a long and complicated journey. A colleague who may want privacy now may later approach you once they have had more time to process their grief, but only if you have conveyed your availability earlier. Here are some dos and don’ts to signal your wanting to keep the door open and render future support.  

Don’ts: These might close off any future conversations and possibilities to help.

  • Offer to talk if you don’t mean it. One person I interviewed had a colleague offer support, but when she replied months later, “Yes, I’d love to take you up on that virtual catch-up,” there was no reply. That added unnecessary hurt and isolation to what was already a difficult ask in reaching out.
  • Bring up the manner of death. A simple “If you ever want to chat and talk, just know that I am always here to support you” is empathetic while nonintrusive.
  • Make it about you. Saying something like, “I know what you are going through, the same thing happened in my family” shifts the narrative to yourself from the person you are trying to console. Worse, as one mental health professional told me, “Equating your own loss might make your colleague feel like you are minimizing theirs.” 
  • Rush in with early assurances such as, “Don’t worry, it’s going to be OK,” or, “You’re strong, you will get through it.” Your colleague is going through a period of uncertainty that needs to be understood, and empathetic listening is your best way to show support without offering what might be perceived as unhelpful counsel. 
  • Provide a reading list. There are an abundance of books on grief, some specifically pertaining to suicide. However, recommending a book can feel like an assignment, even if well intentioned. As one person I interviewed said, “It started to feel like a cascade of people offering condolences were telling me about a book that I really needed to read. It was overwhelming and also gave me anxiety as to what I should be reading, if at all.”  Recommending a book is on a very thin wire with respect to mental health counseling, so perhaps it’s not the time to signal, “Here’s what you should be doing.”

Do’s: These will signal a strong sense of future availability. 

  • If you are close to the person, and have a friendship that would be sustained even if you were not colleagues, open the door to the future. A simple “I am here if you ever want to talk,” conveys understanding and empathy, and also respects your friend’s sense of privacy. One colleague reached out to me with such an offer six months after my father’s suicide. His counsel was extremely helpful, but if he had made the offer sooner I would have been ill-prepared to accept the kind gesture. 
  • Be a steady listener. In your initial interaction with your colleague, allow them the narrative. Don’t try to finish sentences or overtake the conversation. Whatever they might share, replying with understanding and validation will demonstrate a strong sense of empathy that might be very helpful over time.
  • Offer resources, but prepare first. Many organizations offer a range of mental health support resources that can be helpful, including employee assistance programs and specific grief support and counseling access. One corporate leader explained that their company has trained mental health aides who are third-party certified to support those who are grieving. These are all helpful, but in your approach to your colleague, a good start might be, “I know we have good support and counseling resources here. If you need help finding them, or even if you want me to go to HR with you to help find where to start, just let me know.” That way, you are not overwhelming them with what might be multiple options, but just offering support without intrusion. 
  • Offer to talk outside the office. Taking someone out of the office can offer a sense of intimacy without the pressure of office interactions. With such outreach, you are offering what might be the most important thing you can offer: your undivided companionship. And it doesn’t hurt to add, “If now’s not a good time, it’s an offer with no expiry or agenda, just an excuse to get out of the office!” Sometimes a note of levity can bring a moment of relief to such an awful time. You can mention that this opportunity could be during work hours or outside them. Having a conversation after work can reduce the anxiety of feeling, “Well, we have to get back now.” 

Managers Have a Special Responsibility

When a manager has someone on their team who has experienced such a loss, the situation is different from that of a work colleague or acquaintance. As one of the corporate leaders I interviewed told me, “Managers have an obligation to intervene and offer both hard and soft resources.” 

Those could include internal and external support programs, as well as additional time off; temporary reassignment, especially if that person’s role involves travel;  and other gestures such as “What can I take off your plate right now?” 

As a mental health professional told me, “Managers are instrumental in helping to vector the person grieving to the appropriate resources, which also demonstrates a strong organizational duty of care and culture.” As studies demonstrate, a lack of “institutional care” can have a significant impact on a grieving person’s perception of support in the workplace. 

Be present, mindful, and delicate

As someone who is not a mental health professional, you can’t help another person make sense of something that makes no sense. But by being sensitive to the person’s grief in the aftermath of tragedy, you can open the door for them to reach out for companionship, comfort, and even help in finding support.  

And if that ask never comes from your colleague, as long as you were an empathetic listener, it’s not a failure on your part. After such a traumatic experience, each person’s grief narrative is different and it might or might not be something that involves workplace peers, friends, and colleagues. Yet by trying as best you can to follow these strategies, including empathetic listening and validating how your friend is coping, you can provide an opportunity for future interactions without the presumption and pressure that there might be one.
